name: BXP, INC.
moat_justification: Real but narrow: scarce premier gateway locations, the largest premier-workplace platform in the US and a proven development engine are genuine advantages, and the current leasing cycle (occupancy 88.4% and rising, 91.3% leased) shows tenants paying up for the best buildings. But the filed evidence caps the score: gross margin has fallen four straight years to 59.1%, the measurable roic_proxy was only 8.5-8.7% (FY2016-17), GAAP ROE ran 0.3-5.4% in FY2023-25, and the model is capital-hungry ($953M TTM capex) and heavily levered. That is a moderate 5/10, not the sustained well-above-cost-of-capital record a 7+ requires.
fragility_flags: STALE_FY: latest fiscal year ended 10 months ago — check TTM/quarterly OE and consider --base-oe-ps override
NI_OCF_DIVERGENCE: net income and operating cash flow differ by >40% in 2023, 2024, 2025 — find the one-off (tax deposits, impairments, WC swings) before trusting the OE base
SECTOR_MODEL_MISMATCH: Real Estate sector — OE/capex DCF fits real estate names poorly; grade confidence low
WIDE_SCENARIO_SPREAD: super-bull IV is 4.5x super-bear IV — uncertainty is huge; confidence should not be high
BIG_NET_CASH: net cash is 2.6x normalized OE — part of the price is a cash pile, not the operating business; note it in the verdict
one_liner: Largest US premier-office REIT, moat 5/10 — scarce gateway assets and a leasing recovery (occupancy 88.4%, 2026 FFO guided $6.99-$7.05) are real, but on a TTM owner's-earnings base of $1.76/share, after $953M of TTM capex and against $15.63B of filed debt, the weighted IRR is 5.76% (IV@15% $15.10) at $59.12 — it clears the 15% hurdle only below ~$15; the REIT/FFO lens is kinder than the OE lens, but neither supports 15% at this price.
moat_for: Irreplaceable premier-workplace locations in six gateway markets (Boston, New York, San Francisco, Seattle, Washington, DC and Los Angeles) — scarcity, zoning and replacement cost keep competing new supply slow

Scale and integration: the largest publicly traded developer, owner and manager of premier workplaces in the United States, with an in-house development platform that delivered 290 Binney Street (570,000 sq ft, fully leased to AstraZeneca) ahead of schedule and under budget

Leasing momentum and visibility: ~1.8M sq ft leased in Q2 2026 (29% above the 10-year quarterly average), total portfolio occupancy up three straight quarters to 88.4%, leased rate 91.3% with most commencements due before year-end 2026

Pricing power in the tightest submarkets: asking rents rising sharply at trophy assets (e.g. 510 Madison in Manhattan, 680 Folsom in San Francisco) as premier supply stays constrained and AI-driven demand builds
moat_against: Hybrid work is a secular demand headwind for office as an asset class — total portfolio occupancy was still only 88.4% in Q2 2026, six years after the pandemic
Gross margin has eroded four straight years (62.8% FY2021 to 59.1% FY2025 and 59.1% TTM, fundamentals.json) — no demonstrated pricing power at the portfolio level

Returns are thin: the roic_proxy series is measurable only in FY2016-17 (8.7% / 8.5%) because the filer's operating-income tag stops after FY2017, and GAAP ROE ran 3.2% / 0.3% / 5.4% in FY2023-25 — near, not well above, the cost of capital
Capital intensity consumes the cash flow: capex was $900,437,000 in FY2025 and $953,249,000 TTM (ttm.json), and management expects 2026 leasing capital alone nearer $500M

Leverage: $15,633,220,000 of debt on the FY2025 10-K balance sheet (mortgage notes $4,280,067,000 + unsecured senior notes $9,806,100,000 + term loans $797,053,000 + commercial paper $750,000,000) against a $9,391,540,935 market cap — refinancing at higher rates is a standing drag
